Turn Drone Inspections into Usable Solar Defect Evidence

Thematic Area: Solar Inspection & Field Evidence

How might we use drone-based inspections to locate suspected solar-system defects and give technicians clear evidence for follow-up?

Background

An Indonesian solar EPC business has requested drone-based monitoring and maintenance capabilities to strengthen support for its solar installations.

The objective is to collect inspection imagery, locate suspected defects accurately and connect findings with technical follow-up. Relevant startups offer aerial inspections, thermal imaging, 3D site records and inspection-management tools.

A useful solution gives technicians clear locations, equipment context and records they can compare across visits. Solar-specific inspection and engineering interpretation should be built into the service.

Significance of Problem

Without an effective solution, the challenges include:

  • Harder defect follow-up: Inspection images without clear locations or equipment context make findings harder to investigate.
  • Repeated evidence collection: Incomplete records lead to additional evidence-gathering before technicians can plan a response.
  • Slower maintenance decisions: Imagery needs engineering interpretation to establish the cause and urgency of suspected defects.

Existing Efforts

  • Technology priority: Drone-based monitoring and maintenance forms part of the business’s solar technology priorities.
  • Available partner capabilities: An inspection provider creates shared 3D records from site video, with measurement, annotations and optional infrared support. A university building-facade research system locates suspected defects on reconstructed building models, offering a basis for solar-specific adaptation.
  • Collaboration focus: Inspect a selected area and link suspected defects to clear locations and follow-up tasks. Define image quality, reference positions and inspection conditions. Include site permissions, local operating support and solar engineering interpretation in the trial.

Potential Market Size

  • Solar inspection asset base: Global PV capacity reached 2.96 TW at end-2025, following approximately 690 GW of additions during the year. This expanding installed base creates ongoing inspection and maintenance work.

Eligibility / Qualification

  • Technology readiness: Minimum technology readiness level 3 (TRL3).
  • NUS linkage: NUS student or graduate founder, or incubation through an NUS programme such as BLOCK71.
  • Local and overseas startups: Open to Indonesian and overseas startups.
  • Commitment: Complete the selection process and travel to Indonesia if selected.
